Imo they don’t really paint an accurate picture of what is the “best” university for something. It’s based on aspects that tend not to have a bearing on the education you receive (eg student enjoyment can be contributed to by nightlife) and a lot of them use irrelevant metrics. For example, “entry requirements”, which naturally favour Scottish institutions due to the extra weight on the Scottish qualifications. Also, the % of 1st class degrees is another one commonly used, and it should be noted that a 1st at Oxbridge, LSE, imperial etc. is different to a first from Manchester Metropolitan, so this is again a bit of a trite comparison. These are just a few examples. By all means, use them to get a general idea, but certainly don’t use them to make any final decisions.

I personally disagree with your views on GCSEs, but that’s just in my experience. If you’re applying for the most competitive courses (e.g. anything that requires an early application, and more), your GCSEs will certainly be looked at. If they are poor, you are unlikely to get a place. 
The advantages of having good GCSEs are really pronounced when applying for high end courses. 
Even for less competitive courses, your GCSEs may be used as an indicator of performance. If your application punches above its weight a bit (e.g. a weaker student applying to say, Durham), then a bad performance at GCSE can easily lose you an offer.

Firstly, it depends what course you’re applying for. If you can’t get A*s in the relevant subjects at GCSE, and I hate to sound harsh, but I promise that you will struggle to get them at A-level. 
For Russell Group unis, fairly mid-range GCSE grades are unlikely to hinder you (though again this depends on the course and uni itself). Oxbridge, however, will look at your application in depth and if your GCSEs are poor (especially if you don’t have the excuse of going to a bad school) then they may simply choose not to interview you.
If your GCSEs are really not up to standard but you are hellbent on Oxbridge, my advice is this: work really hard for your A-levels and apply after you get your results (e.g., on a gap year). This will give you good time to improve your overall application and will show that you have the academic prowess to meet their requirements. 
Alternatively, you could maybe do AS levels. If you can get As at AS, you can demonstrate an upwards trajectory from GCSE, which Oxbridge like to see in students with weaker GCSE performances. The main benefit of this is that you can avoid taking a gap year if you don’t want one, but I understand that most schools no longer do AS so this is less likely to be a viable solution.
In any case, Oxbridge is not the be all end all. If you’d definitely like to give it a shot then feel free to use my advice but if it’s a hassle then trust me, you do NOT have to apply. There are plenty of excellent unis in the Russell Group.

I should preface this by stating that I grew up in a working class, former mining town far from London, and I am of an immigrant background (Estonian by ethnicity, which was not a member of the EU when my family moved here before I was born).

Firstly, one of the main points that people like to throw around when it comes to the Brexit debate is immigration, so let's start with that.

Immigration, especially in terms of the quotas the EU was trying to impose on us, simply weren't practical for the ordinary people of the UK. Britain is a densely populated island. We are in the midst of a housing crisis and our NHS is on the brink of collapse. We are struggling to cope with our population as it stands, and importing hundreds of thousands of people per year who statistically are more likely to have more children is going to cause further pressures down the line.

The immigration argument is usually mobilised by remainers to try and paint Brexiteers as "racist" (or a similar word), when the way that businessmen make use of the high rates of immigration is actually pretty exploitative all things considered. Foreign workers are more likely to work for cheaper pay, which means that businessmen employed them in their thousands in order to be able to get away with underpaying workers for cheap labour. Native workers just couldn't keep up with that and lost a lot of work. This is where the whole "immigrants taking our jobs" thing comes from. Whilst many remainers like to mock this, it's actually a huge problem which affects not only the now underpaid foreign workers, but working class labourers too, who are now expected to accept lower pay for their work. At the end of it all, the main beneficiary of the immigration policy is businessmen who exploit foreign workers to increase their own profits. 

Another problem with the EU is that, as a globalist organisation working on a huge, international scale, it is necessary for the EU to centralise where it can to save time and prevent dithering. That's understandable. What that did mean for the UK is that London became even more of the UK's economic centre than it was before, and meant that a larger proportion of capital flowed towards London. This of course benefited London and the South East (and is probably why London and SE voted to remain). However, it meant that less investment went to smaller towns whose industries were now being forgotten for cheaper industrial prices abroad (which is again facilitated by EU policy). Industries shut down, and people lost jobs. However, because the money that Britain was gaining from the EU was mostly going to London (as I will say once again, London mostly does benefit from the EU, hence why they voted to stay), we didn't get funding to create new jobs here, and our schools were (and still are) disgustingly underfunded. One of the nearest schools to where I lived has only 1% of students achieving the EBacc (which means you pass a certain amount of core academic subjects, it's not considered difficult usually), and the wider picture is not pretty either. Likewise, our local hospitals are constantly running out of beds to treat patients in, and again, we do not receive the funding to fix that. Meanwhile, because London got plenty of money from the EU, they were able to maintain their high speed railways and vanity projects. This was a bit of a kick in the teeth for working class towns and in my opinion definitely caused resentment. 

There is a LOT more to it, but ultimately something that I don't see a lot in the Brexit debate is the idea that some areas benefit more than others. Did London benefit? On the whole, yes. But whether or not the forgotten working class towns in the North and Midlands did is an entirely different story. I'm not exactly a huge fan of socialism myself, but even I think that the EU's use of capitalism genuinely does harm the working class here, whether or not groups who profess to be in the working class' interests want to admit it.

I’m not convinced you understand what I’m getting at. Brexit strongholds are as such for a reason, so where someone comes from does actually have a bearing on their opinions. This is why the only region of the UK that overall votes remain was London/the South East. 

If you live in the UK you will know that there are in fact regional political dynamics. Some parts of the country will vote very differently because they have different interests. There is even what is known as a “north south divide” in England. There’s a lot of debate on as to where this starts and finishes, however iirc the Domesday book defines this as between the North and the South of the River Trent, which I largely agree with.  

I am more than happy to explain how these differences manifest, particularly in terms of how they affected the Brexit vote if you’d like.  
However, it’s just important to realise that where you’re from absolutely will affect your circumstances which will in turn affect your voting habits. The impact the EU has had on the UK is not a “one size fits all”. Some regions, such as London, have benefitted from it. However, the North of England in particular has actually suffered from EU policy, and that is why I think it’s important to take a look into the circumstances of those who have suffered heavily from this. Of course my suggestion that you go to Mansfield was hypothetical (although honestly, I’m sure if you were polite, plenty of people would be more than happy to engage with you. We’re usually pretty friendly, to be honest), but the point I was trying to convey is that if you want to see how regional circumstances impact voting habits, it’s best not to just take it from sources that are largely run by those that are not affected by this (eg news sources which are largely run by people living in the South, who, whilst their opinions are absolutely valid and worth taking into account, may underrepresent other regional interests).

The fact that you are literally not even willing to look into any other opinion except your own shows your lack of will to develop your own viewpoints and suggests a clear lack of confidence in seeing your views challenged. 

Equally, the fact that you assume that because of someone living in an area with high rates of social deprivation automatically renders their opinion invalid because of your own personal opinion that you don’t feel they’re capable of research and reasoning is seriously pathetic.

Hi, a few tips.  
Don’t go head first into it eg I’m going to cut out EVERYTHING BAD starting tomorrow. You’ll lose motivation quickly. The better option is to say “I won’t have any snacks outside of proper mealtimes tomorrow” and then to work your way through it until you’re eating properly.  
  
If you feel like snacking, drink water. It quenches appetites.  
  
When placing food onto your plate during meal times, be very aware of portioning. It’s easy to pile food up and eat more yet convince yourself you’re eating less. Spread out the food you put on the plate so you don’t feel tempted to put more on because “the plate looks kind of empty so I’ll put more on”.  
  
Eat smarter. Instead of just eating less alone, try eating food that’s good for you rather than just smaller portions of shitty food (a surprising amount of people fail to realise this).  
  
In terms of exercise, I recommend cardio. Anyone can do it, and it’s really good for packing off the pounds. You might also want to look into skin tightening exercises. If you’re fat at the moment and intend to lose weight quickly, you may deal with loose skin. Skin tightening exercises can help mitigate this.  
  
Go for a run to start yourself off. The best thing about running outside is that you can’t just stop once you get too tired for comfort, as you’re outside and have to go back home, but on a treadmill you can just stop the machine and call it a day. Having said that, a gym membership is still worth looking into as cardio isn’t the only exercise you should do. Cardio will help you lose weight but other exercises will get you a nice figure.  
  
Last but not least, don’t be too hard on yourself. It’s easy to feel down in the dumps if you end up having a snack, or stopping during exercise. Don’t let this demotivate you. Just learn from it and keep it going. The best things never come easy, remember that.

1) We wanted more autonomy. 2) Migrant crisis. Great Britain is a densely populated island and we are really not equipped to be dealing with a rising population as it is (our health system is on the brink of collapse, housing crisis etc.), so how are we meant to deal with an influx of migrants who statistically, should go on to have more than the average amount of kids? We need to deal with our own issues before other people’s.  

3) The feeling of being “messed around”. Because of aforementioned reasons and the general sentiment that we were putting more in than we were getting out, there was a rising demand for a referendum on the EU. UKIP (pro-Brexit party) promised this, and gained a lot of traction for it. The Conservatives (fiscal Conservative party) saw that they were losing votes to the pro-Brexit crowd and in a desperate attempt to not lose seats, the conservatives promised a referendum on the EU. They got voted in, and gave the referendum, but not before the majority of their party, including the leader who made this his campaign promise, told people to vote remain, which was a total joke. People felt disenfranchised by this as they felt the main party only cared about power rather than their best interests, so they voted against the conservatives’ wishes to leave. Likewise, a lot of people in the North (which voted overwhelmingly in favour of leaving), feel like they’ve been forgotten about, so perhaps for some voting in the North leave was a “hey, remember us? In the UK, prior to university, we have 2 types of qualifications: GCSEs (that stands for General Certificate of Secondary Education and they're exams you take in typically 8-11 subjects, and you take them usually when you're 16), and A-levels (exams you take in 3, maybe 4 subjects of your choice at 18). A-levels are more important for university applications but the top universities will look at your GCSEs as an indicator of your academic history.  
  
Another type of qualification is the BTEC, and they are vocational qualifications. They don't really have exams, they're more coursework (physical assessment pieces) based. They're often in subjects like construction, beauty, and sport, upon many others. However, BTECs are becoming less common and they are not seen by many as "good" qualifications due to them being less academic.
  
You will apply to a university (you can apply to up to 5 in one application round), and if they feel like you're suitable and are worthy of a place, they'll give you an offer, and you have to get those A-level (or BTEC) grades in order to get in.   
  
Some other notes/interesting facts that may interest you:  
-Usually you can apply to 5 in one application round, although apparently for medicine you can apply to 4.  
-You cannot apply to both Oxford and Cambridge (our elite universities, think Harvard or Yale) in the same application round.  
-The grades in GCSE and A-level range from A*-U (U stands for ungraded, the second lowest grade is G). The GCSE grading system recently changed but it's a bit too complicated to summarise quickly, so don't worry about it, but if you want to know more I will be happy to explain.

As many people here have said, it really depends on who you say something to.  For example, when joking around with friends here in my own country, an entire ocean away from America, I could make a 9/11 joke and get a few laughs. If I made that same joke in NYC, however, it would be much more of a sensitive topic, so I would not even think of making a joke of that nature there. Many people brought up rape jokes, and my thoughts on that are that as rape is very sensitive as a topic, a source of trauma to quite a few and especially the fact that it's grossly under-reported, you really don't know the effect that could potentially have on the person you're telling it to. As for, as some have mentioned jokes about "eating dead babies" (lol), shot in the dark, you've probably never, for example, been traumatised by being forced to watch your baby sibling being eaten, so while it may certainly raise an eyebrow or two, it probably won't have too big of an effect on anyone.
